findings.title: Public `findMany` method removed without replacement call-sites update
findings.body: The previous public method `InsightsBookingService.findMany(...)` (which executed a Prisma `findMany` using the combined conditions) has been removed entirely and replaced by `getBaseConditions()`, which only returns a `Prisma.Sql` fragment and does not execute any query. Any existing caller of `service.findMany(...)` elsewhere in the codebase (e.g. insights routers/analytics endpoints) will now fail to compile/run since the method no longer exists. The PR only touches the service and its integration test; no other files were updated to use `getBaseConditions()` instead. This is a breaking API change that is not called out or verified against other consumers.

findings.title: Constructor option type loosened, losing compile-time scope validation
findings.body: The constructor parameter type was changed from the strict discriminated union `InsightsBookingServiceOptions` (`zod.infer`) to a new loosely-typed `InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions` with `scope: "user" | "org" | "team"` and an optional `teamId`. This removes compile-time enforcement that `teamId` must be supplied when `scope === "team"`. Previously the discriminated union would catch such mistakes at compile time; now a caller can omit `teamId` for `scope: "team"` and only discover the problem at runtime (silently falling back to `NOTHING_CONDITION`), making bugs harder to catch during development.

findings.title: Org-scope authorization test asserts exact array order from unordered DB query, risking flaky failures
findings.body: The test for org-scope conditions asserts `Prisma.sql` equality with an exact ordering of `teamId`/`userId` arrays: `[testData.org.id, testData.team.id, team2.id, team3.id]` and `[testData.user.id, user2.id, user3.id]`. These arrays are built from `TeamRepository.findAllByParentId` and `MembershipRepository.findAllByTeamIds`, neither of which appear to specify an explicit `orderBy`. Postgres does not guarantee row order without `ORDER BY`, so the resulting arrays may be returned in a different order than expected (especially under parallel test execution or query planner changes), causing this `toEqual` deep-equality assertion on the `Prisma.Sql` object (which also compares the `values` array) to fail intermittently even though the underlying SQL semantics (ANY(...)) are order-independent.

findings.title: Caching behavior tests removed without replacement
findings.body: The previous `describe("Caching", ...)` block, which verified that `getAuthorizationConditions()` and `getFilterConditions()` memoize their results via `cachedAuthConditions`/`cachedFilterConditions`, was deleted in this PR and not replaced with an equivalent test using the new `Prisma.sql` comparisons. The service still implements this caching logic (`insightsBooking.ts` lines 83-95), but there is no longer any integration test asserting that repeated calls return the cached value instead of rebuilding (e.g., re-querying membership/team tables), so a regression in the caching logic would go undetected.

findings.title: Raw SQL fragments reference bare, unqualified column names
findings.body: The SQL fragments built in `buildFilterConditions`, `buildAuthorizationConditions`, `buildOrgAuthorizationCondition`, and `buildTeamAuthorizationCondition` reference unqualified column names such as `"userId"`, `"teamId"`, `"eventTypeId"`, `"eventParentId"`, and `"isTeamBooking"` with no table alias/qualifier. These fragments are intended to be composed into larger raw queries (as shown by the `getBaseConditions()` usage in `$queryRaw`). If the final query joins the `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized` table with any other table that also has columns with these same names (common for `userId`/`teamId`), Postgres will raise an ambiguous-column error, or worse, silently resolve to the wrong table depending on query structure. Previously, using Prisma's object-based `where` clause scoped these fields unambiguously to the `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized` model.
